pageData.title: The Olmec Civilization
pageData.para1: The Olmec Civilization. The Olmecs were the first great civilization of Mesoamerica - often called its 'mother culture.' From roughly 1200 to 400 BC, they flourished in the tropical lowlands of today's Veracruz and Tabasco, on Mexico's Gulf Coast, at a time when most of the Americas knew only villages; they are counted among the cradles of civilization in the Americas. Their first center was San Lorenzo Tenochtitlan; when it declined, they moved to La Venta, with other major sites at Tres Zapotes and Laguna de los Cerros. The Olmecs are famous above all for their colossal heads: massive basalt sculptures, up to several tons each, portraying what are assumed to be individual rulers - the first monumental portraits in the Americas. One head from San Lorenzo stands 1.8 meters tall; a famous seated figure known as 'The Wrestler' shows the same mastery in miniature - Olmec artists were equally at home with six-ton monuments and tiny figurines.
pageData.para2: Much of what defines Mesoamerican civilization appears first with the Olmecs: monumental ceremonial centers, the ballgame, long-distance trade in jade and obsidian, and religious imagery that later cultures would inherit. By about 400 BC the great Olmec centers had been abandoned and the population of the eastern heartland dropped precipitously - but elements of their tradition lived on in successor societies, and the pattern they set of cities, kings, gods, and art became the template for every civilization that followed in Mesoamerica, from the Maya to the Aztecs. For centuries afterward the Olmec heartland saw only intermittent occupation, its former glory remembered by the cultures that inherited its gods and its art. They were, in the truest sense, a cradle of American civilization.

pageData.title: Teotihuacan
pageData.para1: Teotihuacan. Teotihuacan was the first great metropolis of the Americas. Founded around 100 BCE in the highlands near today's Mexico City - it began as a religious center of the Mexican Plateau, its great monuments under continuous construction until about 250 CE - it grew until, at its zenith in the first half of the first millennium CE, it was the largest city in the Americas - around 100,000 people, possibly the sixth-largest city in the world at that epoch. It was not an Aztec city: it predated the Aztec Empire by many centuries, and the Aztecs themselves named it, in awe, 'the place where gods were born.' The city was a planned wonder: the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon - among the most architecturally significant pyramids of the pre-Columbian Americas - rose along the great Avenue of the Dead, while the common people lived in multi-floor apartment compounds unique in the ancient Americas; eighty to ninety percent of the valley's population lived in the city, which covered 21 square kilometers and exported obsidian tools across Mesoamerica.
pageData.para2: Teotihuacan's influence reached astonishing distances: its presence is documented at sites in Veracruz and deep in the Maya region, where it intervened in the dynastic politics of Maya cities - whether it was the center of a territorial empire is debated; its cultural empire is not. Around 550 CE the city's great monuments were sacked and systematically burned - possibly amid the climate catastrophes of those years - and Teotihuacan slowly emptied. But the later peoples of Mexico never forgot it: the Aztecs claimed common ancestry with its builders and made pilgrimages to its ruins, believing the gods had created the universe there.

pageData.title: The Classic Maya
pageData.para1: The Classic Maya. The Classic Maya (c. 250-900 AD) were the most brilliant civilization of the ancient Americas. In the jungles of the Yucatan Peninsula, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras - lands where Maya farmers had grown maize, beans, squash, and chili peppers for millennia, built their first cities by 750 BC, and used hieroglyphic writing by the 3rd century BC - dozens of city-states - Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copan - raised sculpted monuments dated by the Long Count calendar, linked by trade, alliance, and war; the two great rivals, Tikal and Calakmul, fought for supremacy for centuries, and even distant Teotihuacan intervened in Maya dynastic politics. Their achievements were intellectual as much as monumental: the Maya script is the most sophisticated writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, their interlocking ritual calendars and mathematics included one of the earliest explicit uses of zero in human history, and their kings were 'divine kings' thought to mediate between mortals and the supernatural realm, expected to be successful war leaders as well as rulers, though by the Late Classic a growing aristocracy had reduced their once-exclusive power - master artists in jade, obsidian, ceramics, stucco, and painted murals, and practitioners of human sacrifice as part of their religion.
pageData.para2: The literate Maya elite recorded their history and ritual knowledge in screenfold books - only three uncontested examples survive - and on countless stelae and ceramics. In the 9th century the central Maya world collapsed into civil wars and abandoned cities, its population shifting north. But the Maya did not vanish: Chichen Itza rose in the Postclassic north, Maya kingdoms still fought the Spanish into the 17th century - the last Maya city fell only in 1697 - and millions of Maya people, speaking Maya languages, live in the same lands today.

pageData.title: The Zapotec Civilization
pageData.para1: The Zapotec Civilization. The Zapotecs - who called themselves Be'ena'a, 'the People who came from the clouds' - built one of the earliest and longest-lived civilizations of Mesoamerica, flourishing in the Valley of Oaxaca from about 700 BC until the Spanish conquest in 1521: more than two thousand years, and archaeological evidence traces their culture back at least 2,500 years. Their capital was Monte Alban, founded around 700 BC on a flattened mountaintop above the valley: one of the first major cities in Mesoamerica, with monumental buildings, ball courts, tombs, and grave goods including finely worked gold jewelry - the whole great plaza carved from the flattened top of a mountain rising over the valley floor. From it, a Zapotec state dominated the territory of today's Oaxaca for a thousand years, until the capital's role passed to Mitla - whose Palace of Columns still stands - and then to Zaachila, which remained the center until the conquest.
pageData.para2: The Zapotecs were among the pioneers of Mesoamerican civilization's defining arts: their early monuments carry some of the region's first hieroglyphic writing and calendrical dates - among the oldest texts in the Americas - and their influence reached far beyond Oaxaca in trade, art, and ideas. Remarkably, they survived as a people through every upheaval - the fall of Monte Alban around 700 AD, the rise of the Mixtecs, even the Spanish conquest that ended their state's independence in 1521. The modern Zapotec peoples of Oaxaca - still speaking their ancient language and preserving their distinct identity in the same valleys their ancestors ruled from Monte Alban - are their direct descendants, a remarkable continuity that few civilizations anywhere in the world can match.

pageData.title: The Adena & Hopewell Cultures
pageData.para1: The Adena and Hopewell Cultures. Long before Europeans arrived, the woodlands of eastern North America were home to mound-building civilizations. The Adena culture came first; then, from 100 BCE to 500 CE, the Hopewell tradition flourished along the rivers of the Northeast and Midwest - not a single society but a widely dispersed set of populations connected by a common network of trade routes, building on the Adena mortuary tradition - the Hopewell Mound Group in Ohio gives the culture its name, and Ohio was its ceremonial heart. The Hopewell exchange system was vast: at its greatest extent it ran from the northern shores of Lake Ontario to the Crystal River mounds of Florida, and along the waterways - the highways of the ancient world - flowed exotic materials from across what is now the United States: obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from the Great Lakes, marine shells from the Gulf Coast, and mica from the southern Appalachians.
pageData.para2: The Hopewell peoples converted these raw materials into finished art: their carved steatite platform pipes, among other prestige goods, traveled far and wide and have been found as grave goods in burials far outside the Midwest, and their great earthen mounds and geometric earthworks, raised over their dead, remain among the most impressive monuments of ancient North America. The Hopewell network faded around 500 CE, but the mound-builder tradition it represented did not die: centuries later, the Mississippian culture would raise Cahokia, the greatest city of ancient North America, on the foundations these Woodland cultures laid - an unbroken tradition of monumental mound building that spanned well over a thousand years of the continent's ancient history.

pageData.title: The Ancestral Puebloans
pageData.para1: The Ancestral Puebloans. The Ancestral Puebloans were the great civilization of the American Southwest - the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples. They lived across the Colorado Plateau in pit houses, clan houses, grand stone pueblos, and the famous cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, built into canyon walls for defense; three UNESCO World Heritage Sites - Mesa Verde, Chaco Canyon, and Taos Pueblo - preserve their achievement. Their roots run deep - archaeologists trace the culture's emergence back many thousands of years in the Southwest - and their world was connected by a complex network of roads and communities centered on the great houses of Chaco Canyon; the kiva, the circular ceremonial chamber, was the heart of every community, and their architecture itself encoded a sophisticated knowledge of celestial cycles.
pageData.para2: For centuries this civilization flourished in an unforgiving land of mesas and canyons, farming maize where rain was scarce and building their knowledge of the sky into the very alignment of their walls; then, in the 13th century, the great cliff dwellings and canyon cities were abandoned, their people migrating south and east to the pueblos along the Rio Grande where their descendants live today. The older name 'Anasazi' is now avoided: it comes from the Navajo word for 'ancestors of our enemies,' and today's Pueblo peoples consider it derogatory - a reminder that these ruins were never a vanished race's but the homes of a living people's ancestors, whose community at Taos is still inhabited after a thousand years. The cliff dwellings were first brought to wide attention when the rancher Richard Wetherill explored Mesa Verde in 1888-1889, and it was he who applied the Navajo exonym that archaeology later retired.
